current.descent_text: The descent has real potential to ruin your day if you don't study it beforehand. From the topout, reach the notch marked by a slung horn/tree between the westernmost and higher central buttress, make one rappel (two 60m ropes, since a single 60m can fall short) over a chockstone tunnel to a dirty ramp with a small cave, then find the upward-trending gully/ledge system on skier's left (not the loose gully directly below) and follow it around back to the base.

They are two-rope rappels: the party tagged a second 60 m rope to make them, since one 60 m rope doubled reaches only 30 m. No intermediate stations are described, so with one rope, take the walk-off. Only the first anchor is specifically located: a tree up and left of the pitch 5 belay.

current.descent_text: From the topout, walk roughly 100-200 ft along the ridge/east to a minor notch separating the westernmost buttress from the higher central buttress, marked by a slung horn/tree. A single-rope rappel (over a chockstone tunnel that can snag the rope on the pull) drops to a dirty ramp with a small cave. From there, find and follow an upward-trending gully or ledge system on skier's left (do NOT descend directly down the obvious gully below the notch, which is loose and hazardous), curving around back to grassy terrain near the base of the routes. Use a single 70m rope.

current.descent_text: The Direct start rejoins the standard Southwest Buttress after its first two pitches, so the descent is the same as the standard route's: from the top, return to the head of the approach gully and make a single-rope rappel (climbers may need to downclimb or work around an open moat at the bottom). Alternatively, from a large rock on the ridge about 10 meters north of the true summit, a fixed rappel ring and sling anchor lets you make a double-rope (two-strand) rappel down to a steep snow section that still connects to rock, avoiding a direct moat crossing via a snow bridge that has historically stayed solid there. From the bottom of either rappel, descend the glacier back down to the notch/col where you left the McAllister Glacier on approach, then reverse the glacier crossing back to high camp. Because this is a mixed rock/snow/glacier descent with an in-situ ring anchor plus natural gully rappel stations, carry standard rappel backup material (a few slings/cord) in case fixed gear needs supplementing, and reassess the moat/snow-bridge crossing each trip since it is snow-condition dependent and can deteriorate later in the season.

current.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb/scramble a short distance to a large rock/boulder on the ridge about 10 meters north of the true summit, where a fixed rappel ring and sling (recently reported as reinforced with an additional sling) anchors the route's single rappel: a double-rope rappel (both strands, ~60m rope) that lowers you to a steep snow slope which, in normal-season conditions, keeps a solid connection to the rock, so a moat crossing usually isn't required at this point. From the bottom of that rappel, downclimb/glissade the snow slope to the notch at the base of the route - the same notch used on the approach - and reverse the glacier travel back toward camp. Some parties describe an alternate single-rope-length rappel off the top of the summit gully instead of the ridge-boulder station; functionally this is still a one-rappel descent, just from a slightly different anchor. Either way, plan on exactly one rope-length transition, not a multi-pitch rappel sequence - the rest of the descent is downclimbing, scrambling, and glacier travel. Because this is a moderate Grade III+ route rather than a big-wall-style descent, no v-thread or chained-rappel sequence is needed in summer conditions; the main descent hazard is the moat at the base of the route staying open or widening late in the season, which can complicate reconnecting with the glacier.
